approach_variants.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,400 ft), just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 1,600 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The entry is marked: a narrow ledge with a cairn on it leads into the southwest gully. After skirting snow you scramble talus and loose scree to that ledge. A cairn on a narrow ledge is the confirmation; an unmarked scramble straight into a gully is not this route.

Inside the gully the test is colour, and it is both a route-finding and a safety instruction: hug the left side, where the dark rock is solid. Parties call that band the black stairs and it offers cleaner scrambling than the middle of the gully. If you are on pale, rubbly rock, you are in the gut of the couloir and on the loose line.

Expect one short low-fifth pitch low down, then class 3 and 4 in the main gully, steepening near the notch between the summit and the West Tower.

Black Tooth Notch is the upper landmark and it is shared, so it identifies the mountain rather than the route: a foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse, with a fixed sling marking the crux step, and loose rock throughout. The Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge both descend through it; this is the only one of the three that climbs up through it.

And the most useful negative fact is about going down, because that is when it bites: the couloir's mouth opens onto cliffs above a waterfall. Exit left onto easier heather benches rather than continuing straight down. A party that is still descending the fall line when it hears water below has gone too far.
